claims.text: Staged high-temperature annealing followed by controlled slow cooling will selectively coarsen nanoprecipitates in tungsten-based HEAs.
Selective precipitate coarsening will increase the thermal conductivity of tungsten-based HEA intermediates.
The heat treatment will retain enough precipitate dispersion to preserve high-temperature mechanical integrity.
As-cast or as-fabricated tungsten-based HEAs have fine precipitate dispersions.
The initial tungsten-based HEA has suboptimal thermal conductivity.
The proposed intervention uses multi-step annealing at 1100–1300 °C followed by controlled slow cooling.
Plasma-facing service involves temperatures of at least 1000 °C and mechanical stresses.
The relevant nanoprecipitates are coherent and partially coarsen during the proposed treatment.
Partial precipitate coarsening reduces electron scattering.
The remaining coherent precipitates continue to provide mechanical reinforcement.
Changing precipitate size and spacing decreases both phonon and electron scattering.
Reduced phonon and electron scattering improves heat conduction.
Strengthening dispersions support mechanical stability under high thermal loads.
Treated samples will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated as-cast or as-deposited samples.
The conductivity improvement will occur with minimal loss of high-temperature strength and ductility.
Untreated tungsten-based HEA intermediates are currently used between plasma-facing tungsten and heat-sink materials.
Untreated tungsten-based HEA intermediates have lower thermal conductivity under comparable conditions.
The conductivity increase will hold only within a stable precipitate-coarsening range of approximately 1100–1300 °C.
Excessive annealing duration or temperature can cause detrimental grain growth and reduced strength.

contradictions.description: The conditions field broadly states that the hypothesis should hold at temperatures ≥1000 °C, whereas the boundary limits the expected conductivity increase to approximately 1100–1300 °C, leaving 1000–1099 °C inconsistent.
The falsification rule refers to 'stovepipe-treated' samples, an undefined treatment that does not match the staged annealing and slow-cooling intervention.
